title: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Except for certain very minute organisms whose form is set directly by molecular forces, the external form of an organism is accounted for by the ratio between its rates of growth in different directions.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is the ratio between the rates of growth in various directions by which we must account for the external forms of all, save certain very minute, organisms.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Form as a function of growth rates”. Scope: all organisms except very minute ones (e.g. single small cells shaped by surface tension)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.48

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Directional growth and external form are measurable with modern imaging, but Thompson's universal accounting claim exceeds available taxonomic and temporal coverage. Existing data can resolve it in selected developmental systems only.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate spatial directional growth tensors from longitudinal images and test whether integrating their ratios predicts observed external shape trajectories. Predictive failure after measured growth is supplied would refute the relation in a system, while success across diverse taxa would support its restricted form.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Most morphology datasets are cross-sectional rather than longitudinal.

Growth ratios can describe shape change without identifying its cause.

The scope covers nearly all organisms.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Directional growth and external form can be measured on existing growth series for some animals and plants. Because any smooth change of outline can be written as anisotropic growth, most datasets are compatible with the claim and with rivals that emphasize migration or mechanics. Only studies that separate local growth from those other contributions are discriminating, and they are a subset that still has to be assembled.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare external shape change with the ratios of extension along principal directions, excluding the minute organisms the claim sets aside. The informative contrast is with form change produced by rearrangement, cell death, or buckling without local growth differences; pure redescription of every shape change as a growth-rate ratio would not decide the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Paired growth and shape series exist for a minority of organisms.

Growth-rate ratios are often a redescription of the shape change they are asked to explain.
